summary: Revises the Telnet STATUS option, which lets one side ask the other about the state of its Telnet options. It was replaced by RFC 859.

eli5.summary: A remote-login computer can ask the other side what settings it is using. This updates how. A later paper replaced it.

questions: what is the telnet status option
how does telnet status is and send work
subtitle: A 1974 revision of the Telnet STATUS option, which lets each side ask how the other sees its options.

tldr.problem: The earlier STATUS option did not fit the normal Telnet option structure, and simply renegotiating options could cause a nonterminating request loop.
tldr.mechanism: WILL and DO only grant permission to discuss status. The actual exchange happens in subnegotiation: the DO side sends SEND, and the WILL side answers with IS followed by its current options.
tldr.outcome: This revision was obsoleted by RFC 859.

today: RFC 651 was obsoleted by RFC 859, which now defines the Telnet STATUS option.

sections.title: The STATUS Option
sections.content:
The Telnet STATUS option has code 5. It lets a user or process verify the current status of Telnet options (for example echoing) as the other end sees them. Its default is DON'T STATUS / WON'T STATUS, meaning status is not discussed.

The revision lets STATUS fit the normal structure of Telnet options by deferring the transfer of status to the SB command, and it greatly reduces the bytes needed to describe option state.
sections.eli5: It is a way to ask the other computer, "what settings do you think we are using?", without starting an argument about them.

sections.title: Negotiating and Requesting
sections.content:
WILL and DO now only obtain and grant permission for future discussion. After they are exchanged, the sender of WILL STATUS may send status spontaneously or when asked.

Only the sender of DO may send IAC SB STATUS SEND IAC SE (SEND is code 1). Only the sender of WILL may send IAC SB STATUS IS ... IAC SE (IS is code 0). At worst, the information may be sent twice.
sections.eli5: First both sides agree it is okay to talk about settings. Then one side can ask, and only the other side answers.

sections.title: The IS Report
sections.content:
Inside IS, the subcommands WILL, DO and SB are used exactly as in normal option negotiation, except that SB is ended by SE rather than IAC SE. A literal SE data byte is sent doubled (SE SE).

Options not mentioned are assumed to be in their default states, so a single IS report describes the condition of all options. The RFC's example shows a host reporting that it will echo, will not send Go-Ahead, and will both issue and request status.
sections.eli5: The answer is a short list of the settings that are switched on. Anything not on the list is assumed to be at its usual setting.
